title: Europe should fund Ukraine’s defence industry as a partner, not a supplier
gist: Chatham House argues the EU's 2027 €45bn Ukraine loan (€31.7bn for defence) should favour Europe-sited joint ventures with Ukraine's fast-iterating defence industry—whose output grew from ~$1bn (2022) to ~$35bn (2025) but runs at ~40% capacity for lack of orders—rather than treating Ukraine as a supplier, given Kyiv's export limits, ceasefire risk and Russian hybrid threats.

insights.claim: In mid-November 2026 Ukrainian forces destroyed a road span of the Kerch Bridge using jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink, as the seventh phase of an operation that first targeted the crossing's air-defence, radar and electronic warfare systems.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ukraine is fielding sovereign-controlled comms for long-range strike, reducing reliance on Starlink and showing multi-phase precision-strike maturity.
insights.quote: The strike used jet-powered drones and cruise missiles reportedly guided through an airborne relay network rather than Starlink.
insights.locator: In mid-November, Ukrainian forces destroyed

insights.claim: Dutch-headquartered Destinus says its systems were the only foreign-made weapons used in Ukraine's Kerch Bridge strike, and reports output approaching 300 Ruta missiles a month.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Destinus is a visible European-based beneficiary of Ukraine-linked strike demand with meaningful production scale — watch for funding/contract flow.
insights.quote: Destinus reports output approaching 300 Ruta missiles a month
insights.locator: The strike package was not wholly Ukrainian

insights.claim: On 22 November 2026 Kyiv said seven Ukrainian-made sea drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury at the Benghazi naval base in Libya, an attack apparently involving no foreign weapons, demonstrating low-cost long-range maritime capability.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Cheap unmanned maritime systems can now hold naval assets at risk far from Ukraine — relevant to naval procurement and maritime drone makers.
insights.locator: Days later, on 22 November

themes.theme: Speed, not scale, is Ukraine's edge

insights.claim: Ukraine's defence production capacity grew from around $1 billion in 2022 to an estimated $35 billion in 2025, versus €418 billion of combined EU member-state defence spending that year, so Ukraine's edge is innovation speed rather than scale.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ukraine's industry is a fast-growing but small player relative to EU budgets — value lies in its iteration speed and know-how, not volume.
insights.quote: Its production capacity has grown from around $1 billion in 2022 to an estimated $35 billion in 2025.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s innovation advantage

insights.claim: Testing weapons in an active warzone gives Ukrainian defence firms immediate operational feedback and compressed procurement cycles, letting them design, field and adapt systems in months rather than the years typical of European procurement.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Combat-tested iteration is a structural advantage European primes cannot replicate in peacetime; partnering is the way to access it.
insights.quote: design, field and adapt systems in months, rather than the years typical of European procurement
insights.locator: Sequencing of that kind

insights.claim: War has given Ukraine's defence industry urgency, a tolerance for failure and feedback loops measured in days, and with Kyiv stripping out procurement, testing and regulatory barriers this has delivered interceptor drones and long-range strike at a pace and cost European procurement has struggled to match.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect pressure on European procurement reform and on incumbents' cost/timeline structures in drones and strike.
insights.quote: urgency, a tolerance for failure, and feedback loops that are measured in days
insights.locator: The war has given Ukraine’s defence industry

insights.claim: Operational effectiveness should not be confused with industrial capacity: the assumption that Ukraine can build anything Europe needs, including air defence, if funded is a tempting but flawed conclusion.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Don't extrapolate Ukraine's drone success to high-end systems like ballistic-missile defence; European suppliers retain that niche.
insights.quote: operational effectiveness should not be confused with industrial capacity
insights.locator: The tempting conclusion is

insights.claim: Know-how is not Ukraine's main constraint — it inherited much of the Soviet missile-design base and is developing ballistic and anti-ballistic missiles alongside unmanned systems; the binding constraints are capital, production capacity, facilities vulnerable to Russian attack, and specialist components such as advanced electronics and seekers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Bottlenecks in electronics and seekers point to supply-chain opportunities for European component makers.
insights.locator: Know-how is not the main constraint

insights.claim: According to the head of Ukraine's Council of Defence Industry, manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders, suggesting additional funding could quickly unlock production.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Finance is the most immediate constraint — new EU money could translate into output rapidly given ~60% idle capacity.
insights.quote: manufacturers are operating at around 40 per cent of their potential capacity because the government is not placing enough orders
insights.locator: The head of Ukraine’s Council of Defence Industry

insights.claim: Advanced air defence, especially against ballistic missiles, depends on complex radar and sensor networks, high-end interceptors and supply chains needing sustained investment, so Ukraine's experience cannot remove Europe's need to build and maintain such capabilities itself.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Supports continued European investment in radar, sensors and high-end interceptors regardless of Ukraine partnerships.
insights.locator: However, Europe’s requirements go beyond volume

insights.claim: Ukraine's export framework protects its own forces: firms may export only if they can also fulfil Ukrainian government contracts, exports carry no intellectual property rights, and re-export requires Kyiv's approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: European buyers cannot count on Ukrainian supply or IP; this caps the value of a pure supplier relationship.
insights.quote: re-export requires Kyiv’s approval and attracts a 20 per cent tax
insights.locator: The limits of a supplier relationship

insights.claim: Even drones built at the first Ukrainian joint venture in Germany are currently allocated to Ukraine's armed forces, so in a crisis European governments could not assume Ukrainian output would be available for their own needs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Supply-security risk for Europe-based Ukrainian JV output until allocation rules change.
insights.locator: Even the drones built at the first

insights.claim: A ceasefire would erode Ukraine's defence-innovation advantage by reducing the operational feedback, procurement incentives and pressure that drive it, so European planning should not assume the wartime model persists or that Ukraine's priorities stay aligned with Europe's.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A settlement is a risk to the Ukraine defence-tech thesis; value the partnership on technology transfer, not perpetual wartime iteration.
insights.locator: A ceasefire would raise a different problem

themes.theme: Russian hybrid pressure on joint production

insights.claim: Russia treats European support for Ukrainian defence production as participation in the war: its embassy in The Hague publicly asked whether the Netherlands had joined the war after the Destinus-supported strike, and Russia has named European firms producing drones for Ukraine as potential targets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Firms hosting Ukrainian-linked production face diplomatic coercion and physical-security risk — a cost to price in.
insights.locator: Closer cooperation also carries political risk

insights.claim: In August 2026 an explosive-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport, an attack Germany has attributed to Russia; such hybrid attacks could make some European governments more cautious about hosting joint production.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Hybrid threats may slow JV siting decisions and raise security spending on facilities, personnel and supply chains.
insights.quote: an explosive-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport
insights.locator: In August, an explosive-laden drone

themes.theme: EU 2027 loan: fund partnership, not supply

insights.claim: The European Commission's proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027 — the second half of the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan — includes €31.7 billion for defence, and its allocation will have long-term consequences beyond Ukraine's immediate military needs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A €31.7bn defence pot is a major demand driver; how it splits between Ukrainian, joint-venture and non-European (incl. US) procurement determines winners.
insights.locator: From procurement to partnership

insights.claim: Of three uses for EU funds — buying Ukrainian output, buying from outside Europe (including the US where a derogation allows), or funding joint ventures on European territory — only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe, so a meaningful share of the package should go to them, while air defence for Ukraine this winter remains central.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Argues for policy tilting EU defence money toward Europe-sited Ukrainian JVs, potentially at the expense of US suppliers.
insights.quote: But only joint ventures build enduring capacity across Europe.
insights.locator: Funding can support Ukrainian production

insights.claim: A Ukraine-Europe defence partnership should rest on a division of labour: Ukraine brings low-cost mass production, rapid iteration and near-combat testing via its state-backed Brave1 cluster, while Europe brings radar and sensors, high-end interceptors, sovereign space-based communications, capital, and production sites beyond the reach of Russian missiles.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Maps where each side's companies add value — European sensor, interceptor and space-comms firms are natural JV partners.
insights.locator: European states and companies, in turn

insights.claim: Joint ventures will only work with genuine technology transfer, shared research, integrated supply chains, allocation priority agreements, predictable multi-year financing and IP agreements; Ukrainian reporting describes the German joint venture as closer to a showcase than the start of a systematic process.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for multi-year financing and IP frameworks as the signal that JVs move from showcase to scale.
insights.quote: closer to a showcase than the start of a systematic process
insights.locator: Joint ventures and licensed production

insights.claim: Treating Ukraine merely as a source of weapons risks creating a dependency that becomes visible only when European security is next under pressure, whereas shared industrial capacity strengthens both Ukraine's defence and Europe's resilience.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames the policy debate: expect advocacy for co-production over off-the-shelf purchasing in EU defence financing.
insights.quote: Treating Ukraine as a source of weapons risks creating a dependency that becomes visible only when European security is next under pressure.
